titulo: Say it again, slower — and write it down for me
subtitulo: The three words that hand the conversation back to the other person and buy you another go
cena: You are at a Renfe ticket window, the woman has just fired a whole sentence at you, you caught one word of it, and there are four people behind you.

clique.desconto: Nobody handed you those six sentences. You built all six out of one, in about eleven minutes.
clique.piso: Most people spend a fortnight here and never once ask a stranger to slow down. You will do it before lunch on day one.

permissao: You are allowed to ask the same person the same thing four times. Nobody there is marking your comprehension, and the traveller who asks is the one who gets helped.
frasePiso: You will get a stranger to slow down, say it again, and put it on paper. Most people who spend a fortnight in Spain never ask once.
espelho: The polite two-second gap you leave before answering is the bit that reads as odd there. It lands as hesitation, not as manners, and somebody fills it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You start your sentence with a run-up — sorry, I was wondering whether you could possibly — and the answer arrives before you have finished, or the other person turns to somebody else.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I was being polite and I got cut off. Either I was rude, or he was, and either way I have lost my turn.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The padding is what did it. A request there is short and the courtesy sits in your tone and in one 'por favor' at the end — five layers of hedging make the listener lose the thread of what you actually want (docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §3.4).
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Lead with the three words, put the job on the end, and stop. Do not wait for a gap before you go in — it is not coming.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the repeat instead of losing your turn, and you stop being the foreigner who only listens.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not with the Guardia Civil, at a bank counter or in front of a doctor. There the extra layer costs you nothing, people take turns, and usted is the right call.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Spain reads English better than it speaks it. The hotel desk manages; the ticket window often does not.

steps.pt: Part three. Warm-up. Palm flat. Hold each vowel two seconds. Ah. Eh. Ee. Oh. Oo. If the hand tilts, the vowel slid.

steps.promptPt: The same proper old place as yesterday, the same waiter in the white jacket, and he is seventy and unhurried. Get his attention and order your milky coffee. Speak now.
steps.es: Perdone, ¿me pone un café con leche, por favor?
steps.pinyin: pehr-DOH-neh, meh POH-neh oon kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Excuse me, could I have a white coffee, please?
Right. New scene. A Renfe ticket window. She fires one long sentence at you. You caught one word. Four people behind you.
And your brain stops. That is not failure, that is Tuesday. Everyone who learns a language stands there with that face on.
So here is the permission, and I mean it. You are not going to understand the fast bit. Ask once, smile, and carry on.
What you need is a repair kit. Three rungs, one sentence, three hats. First, the two that open the door.
I speak a little Spanish. — Silent H, and that Ñ is the middle of 'onion'.

steps.promptPt: Back at that ticket window, before she gives up on you and switches to English. Buy yourself a bit of patience. Speak now.
steps.pt: I speak a little Spanish.
Now the English question. Spain reads English better than it speaks it. The hotel desk manages; the ticket window often does not.
So ask it second, never first. Two words of theirs before it changes the whole temperature of the exchange.
Do you speak English? — Silent H again. The punch lands on the last beat: in-GLEHS.

steps.promptPt: You have tried twice in his language and it is not landing — and this is the man about to tow your hire car. Time to ask. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do you speak English?
And now the frame that repairs the rest. In English: can you, for me. Three little words, then the job you want doing.
Can you say that again for me, please? — The frame is the first three words. The last one is the job.
Those three words never move. The last one is the piece that changes, and it goes in as the dictionary has it.

steps.promptPt: The pharmacy counter. He has told you the dose twice, fast, and you have honestly no idea what he said. Ask him for it one more time. Speak now.
steps.pt: one more time

steps.es: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh ah-BLAR mahs dehs-PAH-thyoh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Can you speak more slowly for me, please? — 'Despacio' carries that free 'th': dehs-PAH-thyoh.
steps.tts: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?

steps.promptPt: The ticket window, and she has started. It is coming out as one unbroken stream with no edges in it. Stop her and set the pace yourself. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh ah-BLAR mahs dehs-PAH-thyoh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: set the pace
Third one, and it is the one that saves your day. When the words will not work, stop using words. Get it onto paper.

steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh ehs-kree-BEER, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Can you write it down for me, please? — Same three words at the front. This one rescues prices, addresses, times and the name of a medicine.

steps.promptPt: The hotel desk. She has just said a street name with four beats in it that you will not hold for ten seconds. Get it onto paper. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh ehs-kree-BEER, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: onto paper

steps.es: ¿En el móvil o en un papel?
steps.pinyin: en el MOH-beel oh en oon pah-PEL
steps.pt: 👂 'On your phone or on paper?' — the question that comes straight back at you. It wants one word.
steps.tts: ¿En el móvil o en un papel?

steps.promptPt: She has the pen in her hand and she wants to know where it goes. Your phone dies at four every afternoon. Answer her. Speak now.
steps.pt: the old-fashioned one, please
Same three words, new job. And watch how far they carry you outside a repair.

steps.promptPt: Half eleven at night, the restaurant is putting chairs on tables, it is raining and the square outside is empty. Ask the waiter to sort you a ride home. Speak now.
steps.pt: a ride home

steps.promptPt: The machine at the station has swallowed your card, and there is a woman in a Renfe waistcoat two metres away looking at her phone. Three words. Speak now.
steps.pt: three words that fetch a human
And the last one, for what you cannot say at all. Stop talking, hold out the screen, ask for a finger on it.

steps.promptPt: He has answered with three streets, two roundabouts and a long sweep of the arm. You have his goodwill and nothing else. Put his finger on your screen. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?
steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh en-seh-NYAR en el MAH-pah
steps.pt: on the screen, not in words
steps.tts: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?

steps.pt: In part eight you learn to ask where things are. That one is the reason you will survive the answer.
I do not understand. Sorry, what? — Two short ones for when a whole sentence is too much sentence.

steps.promptPt: Three exchanges deep and the thread has gone entirely. Say so, plainly, and hand it back to him. Speak now.
steps.pt: I do not understand. Sorry, what?
One thing to notice at the counter, because it decides whether any of this lands.
You take a run-up. Sorry, I was wondering whether you could possibly. And he answers before you finish, or turns to somebody else.
The padding did that. Lead with the three words, put the job on the end, and stop. Your 'por favor' goes at the back, once.
Do not wait for a gap. It is not coming. Where that does not hold: a doctor, a bank counter, the Guardia Civil.
The mirror. That polite two-second pause before you answer reads as hesitation there, and somebody fills it.
So the padding matters more than the accent. A short, blunt sentence gets answered. A beautiful long one does not.
And you are allowed to ask the same person the same thing four times. Nobody there is marking your comprehension.
The traveller who asks four times gets helped. The one who nods and understood nothing ends up on the wrong train.

steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh ehs-kree-BEER, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Say it with her, over the top. This is the one you will want on day one.

steps.es: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh ah-BLAR mahs dehs-PAH-thyoh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: And this one. Loud enough that she hears it over the queue.
Count them. The ticket window, the pharmacy counter, the hotel desk, the restaurant, the station and the street.
Nobody handed you six sentences. You built all six out of one, and the only thing that moved was the last word.
Most people spend a fortnight here and never once ask a stranger to slow down. You will do it before lunch on day one.
Out loud, all three. Can you say that again for me. Can you speak more slowly for me. Can you write it down for me.
Part three done. Next, the one with a deadline on it: the four things to sort out before you fly. Hasta luego.
👂 'No harm done.' — what comes back when you apologise for your Spanish. Believe it, and carry on.

secoes.titulo: The three rungs, and the two openers
secoes.corpo: Everything in this part hangs off one opening: '¿me puede…?' — literally 'can you, for me'. What follows it is the job, and it goes in exactly as the dictionary gives it: repetir, hablar más despacio, escribir, ayudar, llamar un taxi, enseñar. Where the thing being repeated is already obvious — a price, a street name, a platform — the little 'lo' slides in: '¿me lo puede escribir?', '¿me lo puede enseñar?'. Treat 'me lo puede' as one word and stop looking at it. The two openers that come before the ladder are 'hablo un poco de español', which asks for patience instead of ending the conversation, and '¿habla inglés?', which is asked second and never first.

exemplos.pt: Can you say that again for me? — rung one

exemplos.es: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
exemplos.pt: Can you speak more slowly for me? — rung two
Can you write it down for me? — rung three, and the one that ends the problem
Can you help me? — three words, fetches a human
Can you call me a taxi?

exemplos.es: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?
exemplos.pt: Can you show me on the map?

secoes.titulo: 'Puede' or 'puedes' — and why we only gave you one
secoes.corpo: Spain runs on 'tú' far more than the Spanish taught to Americans suggests: bars, shops, taxis, anyone your own age or younger. Save 'usted' for three places — police and officials, someone clearly elderly, and a formal counter. The catch is that the repair kit gets used precisely at those counters, and under pressure, which is why we gave you the 'usted' shape and left it there: '¿me puede…?' is correct with absolutely everybody, and nobody in Spain has ever been offended by it. If the person is young and relaxed you will hear '¿me puedes…?' come back at you, and it means the same thing. Do not stop to convert it.

exemplos.pt: Can you, for me…? — usted / tú

secoes.titulo: When words fail: use the artefact
secoes.corpo: The most reliable communication tool you own is not a sentence, it is your phone screen and a pen. Show the address rather than pronouncing it. Show the booking rather than describing it. Have the price written down rather than decoding a number said fast. Have the pharmacist write the name of the medicine. Each of those moves the risk off your pronunciation and onto paper, and paper never mishears anything. A machine translator belongs here too, and there is no shame in it: type it, turn the screen round, and let them read. The sentence that unlocks the whole category is the third rung — '¿me lo puede escribir, por favor?'.

exemplos.pt: Can you write it down for me, please?

exemplos.es: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?
exemplos.pt: Can you show me on the map?
On paper, please. — the answer when they offer your phone instead

secoes.titulo: Why the padding costs you the answer
secoes.corpo: A request in Spain is short, and the courtesy lives in your tone and in one 'por favor' at the end rather than in five layers of 'would you mind'. Translate an English run-up literally and two things happen: the listener loses the thread of what you actually want, and the extra seconds are read as distance rather than as manners. This is the trap that hits the British traveller hardest, and it is not a rule about being rude — it is a rule about being heard. Drop the run-up, raise the volume a notch above what feels polite at home, and go in without waiting for a gap. The gap is not scheduled. Where this reverses: a doctor, a bank counter and anyone in uniform, where turns are taken properly and the longer form costs you nothing.
